title: CQRS, RAG, Monoliths and Microservices
oneLiner: Four architectural ideas: separate writing from reading (CQRS), feed an LLM your own documents (RAG), and decide whether to ship one big app or many small services.

what.html:
CQRS splits a system into a part that changes things (commands) and a part that reads things (queries). RAG lets a language model answer from your own documents by retrieving relevant passages first. Monoliths put everything in one deployable app; microservices split it into small services that scale and deploy independently.

Everyday versionA library has a back office that adds and catalogues books (commands) and a front desk that answers questions (queries); the front desk's list is updated a little later. When you ask a question, the librarian first finds the right pages (retrieval) and then answers from them (generation).

why.html:
• Training and serving have very different load patterns; separating them lets each scale on its own.
  • LLMs don't know your company's documents or today's facts; RAG gives them the right context without retraining.
  • A single app is easy to start but hard to scale and change; services are the opposite.
  • Choosing the wrong structure early makes later growth expensive.

how.title: Commands vs queries
how.html: A method should either do something (command) or tell you something (query), never both. In web APIs, GET is a query; POST, PUT and DELETE are commands. Taken further, writes and reads can use separate stores, avoiding lock contention.

how.title: Eventually the same everywhere
how.html: In ML, the command side trains and registers models; the query side serves predictions and dashboards. They sync through an event stream, so for a few minutes after a new model is released some regions still serve the old one. That's eventual consistency.

how.title: What RAG does
how.html: Before answering, find the passages that matter and paste them into the prompt. The model answers from fresh or private facts and makes fewer things up, without retraining. Ingestion (chunk, embed, index) is one pipeline; answering (embed the question, search, build the prompt, generate) is another.

how.title: The parts of a RAG system
how.html: A framework such as LangChain glues the steps together. An embedding model turns text into vectors where similar meanings sit close together. A vector store (Pinecone, FAISS, Chroma) finds the nearest chunks quickly using indexes like HNSW.

how.title: The monolith
how.html: One app, one database, one deployment. Fast in-memory calls, easy to test and deploy. But you can only scale the whole thing, adopting new tech means rewrites, and one crash takes everything down. A model plus its API in one Flask app is a monolithic ML service: great for prototypes.

how.title: Microservices
how.html: Split the app into services that each do one job and own their data, behind an API gateway. Each can be deployed many times a day, use its own technology, and scale independently. "Gather together the things that change for the same reasons; separate those that change for different reasons."

how.title: Microservices for ML
how.html: A gateway routes requests, a model service only predicts, a logging service only records. When prediction traffic grows, add model-service copies; if logging crashes, predictions continue. The price: network calls, more deployments, harder debugging.

demo.html: Pick a question and watch the retriever choose chunks from four company policies. Shrink the chunk size until a number gets separated from its meaning; grow it until irrelevant text crowds the prompt. Raise top-k to see how much context the model would have to read.

example.html:
HR assistant for a 5,000-person company. Policies are chunked, embedded and indexed nightly (command side). Employees' questions are embedded, matched against the index and answered with citations (query side). A policy updated at 9 am is answerable once the nightly job has run (eventual consistency), so urgent changes trigger an immediate re-index. The assistant starts as a single FastAPI app; when usage grows, the embedding/retrieval service and the LLM gateway are split into separate services so the expensive LLM calls can scale separately.

Supplementary If a question isn't covered ("parental leave" when no such policy is indexed), retrieval still returns the "closest" chunks; the prompt must tell the model to say it doesn't know.

misunderstandings: It separates responsibilities; separate stores are optional.
Eventual consistency means data is wrong.
It's temporarily out of date and converges; fine for many ML uses.
It reduces them; bad retrieval or ignored context still causes errors.
Bigger chunks are always better context.
Too big adds noise and cost; too small splits facts from meaning.
Microservices are always the right choice.
They add network and operations cost; monoliths suit prototypes and small teams.
takeaways: CQRS separates commands (state changes) from queries (reads), possibly with separate stores synced by events.
In ML, the command side trains/registers and the query side serves; they are eventually consistent.
RAG = retrieve relevant chunks + augment the prompt + generate; it is pipe-and-filter plus CQRS.
Embeddings and vector stores (with indexes such as HNSW) make retrieval fast.
Monoliths are simple but scale and change as one block; microservices give independent scaling and deployment at an operational cost.
thirty: CQRS separates operations that change state, commands, from operations that read it, queries; in APIs, GET is a query and POST, PUT and DELETE are commands, and writes and reads can use separate stores connected by events, which makes the system eventually consistent. In ML, the command side trains and registers models while the query side serves predictions, so a new model reaches all regions after a short delay. RAG grounds an LLM in your own documents: an ingestion pipeline chunks, embeds and indexes documents in a vector store, and a query pipeline embeds the question, retrieves similar chunks and builds the prompt. That makes RAG pipe-and-filter plus CQRS. Finally, a monolith deploys everything as one unit, which is simple but scales as a block, while microservices split responsibilities into independently scalable services at the cost of operational complexity.
